senses.gloss:
Dvādaśāha
(‘[a sacrifice extending over] twelve days’)
------------------------------------------
The द्वादशाह is a Vedic sacrifice belonging to the सोमयाग group. It is called so since it extends over twelve (= dvādaśa) days. It can be either an अहीन (spread over several days) or a sattra (where the yajamānas themselves are the priests too).
It comprises Daśāha (ten principle days) preceded and followed by an अतिरात्र. (See ATIRĀTRA.) The Daśāha again has a few minor सोम sacrifices like the Pṛṣṭhya and the Ukthya. The details are too many and complicated.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.

dvāradevatā
(‘door-goddess’)
------------------------------------------
Along with the dikpālas or दिक्पालकस् (guardian deities of directions), the tāntrik works like the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra mention fifteen dvāradevatās or gods and goddesses guarding doors and doorways. Some of them are: Padmā, भारती, दुर्गा, Manobhavā, Vasantā, गङ्गा, Vīra-vighneśa and Dhātā.
They guard the doors of the temples of मोथेर्-goddess.

dvayamantra
(‘mantra in two parts’)
------------------------------------------
In Śrīvaiṣṇavism—the practical religious aspect of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta—prapatti or शरणागति (total surrender to God) is a very important step of spiritual practice.
In प्रपत्ति, one has to receive three mantras or sacred formulae from a compe-tent आचार्य (spiritual preceptor). The first is the aṣṭākṣarīmantra (the eight-syllabled मन्त्र) viz., oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya. The second is the dvaya or द्वयमन्त्र, a twofold मन्त्र. The third is the चरमश्लोक, the 66th śloka of the 18th chapter of the Bhagavadgītā (‘sarva-dharmān parityajya...’).
The द्वयमन्त्र is:
1. śrīman-नारायण-caraṇau śaraṇaṁ prapadye ।
2. śrīmate nārāyaṇāya namaḥ ।
The first मन्त्र means: ‘I take refuge at the feet of Śrī-नारायण’.
The second one means: ‘Obeisance to Śrī-नारायण.’
In both the mantras नारायण is described as being with Śrī or लक्ष्मी.
Though the commentators declare that these mantras are part of the Kaṭhaśruti, the recensions available now do not contain them.
This द्वयमन्त्र is called ‘mantra-ratna’ and is considered a tāntrik मन्त्र. Hence all have the right to receive it for spiritual evolution.
See also RAHASYATRAYASĀRA.

Dvāparayuga
(‘the yuga [which comes] after the second; [viz., the third]’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu Mythological lore, time is expressed in immense quantities. A कल्प is a day of ब्रह्मा, the creator. It is divided into 14 manvantaras and also into 1000 चतुर्युगस्. The चतुर्युगस् are: कृतयुग, त्रेतायुग, द्वापरयुग and कलियुग. Thus, the द्वापरयुग is the third of the four युगस्. Its duration is 8,64,000 human years.
See YUGAS for details.

dvārapālas
(‘guardians of doors’)
------------------------------------------
All the हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् built in the traditional style have द्वारपालस् or door-guardians, generally at the sides of the main doorway of the sanctum. Their iconographic details vary according to the sectarian affiliation of the temple (Śaiva, शाक्त or Vaiṣṇava).
In Vaiṣṇava temples there are three pairs of द्वारपालस्: Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the sides of the temple; जय and विजय at the sides of the sanctum in the ardhamaṇḍapa; Pūrṇa and पुष्कर at the outside enclosure. Sometimes नन्द and Sunanda, as also Kumuda and Kumudākṣa are also mentioned as द्वारपालस्.
There are other deities also who too function as guardians. For instance गरुड, विष्वक्सेन, आनन्द, Vīrasena and Sambhava.
In the शिव temples the following four-armed guardians are shown: नन्दि to the left and महाकाल to the right of the eastern entrance; विनायक and Puṇḍarīka at the southern entrance; Vṛṣabha and स्कन्द at the western entrance; देवी and चण्डेश्वर at the northern entrance.
Daṇḍi, Muṇḍi, Āmoda, Pramoda and क्षेत्रपाल are the other deities mentioned as guardians in शिव temples.
In the देवी temples the द्वारपालस् are: Vetāla and Karaṭa at the eastern entrance; Piṅgalākṣa and Bhrukuṭa at the southern entrance; Dhūmraka and Kukkuṭa at the western entrance; Raktākṣa and Sulocana at the northern entrance.
Sometimes certain goddesses like Ṣaṣṭi, Kumārī, Dhanadā, Acalā and others are also projected as dvāramātṛkās or guardian deities of entrances.
For temples of other deities like कार्त्तिकेय and गणेश, the द्वारपालस् will be different.

dvādaśī
(‘the twelfth day’)
------------------------------------------
Among the Hindu festivals and sacred days—which are generally celebrated according to the cāndramāna or lunar calendar—ekādaśī and द्वादशी (the eleventh and the twelfth days) are the more common ones, ceremonially observed.
Dvādaśī is the day following एकादशी and hence known for pāraṇā, ceremonial breaking of the fast, which includes worship of विष्णु, celibacy, avoiding a second meal as also non-vegetarian ड़ोओद्. Some of the पुराणस् specially mention eight kinds of dvādaśīs like Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī and Pāpanāśinī, associated with certain nakṣatras (asterisms). ड़स्तिन्ग् is enjoined for these days also.
One of the most well-known festivals that falls on a द्वादशी is the Utthāna-द्वादशी (Kārttīka śukla द्वादशी ). On this day Lord विष्णु who had gone to sleep on the Śayanī day (Āṣāḍha śukla एकादशी ), gets up. Hence it is called ‘Utthānadvādaśī (utthāna = getting up).
It is again on this day that तुलसी or Vṛndā was married to Hari or विष्णु. So, it is also called ‘Tulasīvivāha day.’ Ceremonial मर्रिअगे of the तुलसी plant (holy basil) with Lord Hari is performed on this day. In some houses images of Hari and तुलसी are kept for three days (from the navamī to एकादशी) and worshipped. They are married on the द्वादशी day.
Vaikuṇṭha-द्वादशी or Mukkoṭi-द्वादशी is another festival observed in the South. It is the next day of वैकुण्ठ एकादशी. Details of the festival are the same as for the एकादशी.

Dvārakā
(‘the gateway to [liberation]’)
------------------------------------------
Places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are legion in हिन्दुइस्म्. In the olden days, when transport and communication were difficult, the devout Hindu cherished a life-time’s ambition of visiting important pilgrim centres like काशी or प्रयाग.
द्वारका">Dvārakādhīśa Temple at DvārakāOne of the seven important places of पिल्ग्रिमगे which every Hindu liked to visit in his life, is द्वारका or Dvārikā, also known as ‘Dvārāvatī’. It is situated on the sea-shore, near the Okha port in Saurashtra (Gujarat).
Śrī कृष्ण is said to have built it. It got submerged in the sea at the time of his departure from this world.
Most of the scholars agree that the modern Dwarka along with the Bet-Dwarka (an island in the sea) could have been the same द्वारका described in the Hindu mythological works and digests.
A Viṣṇukṣetra (place dear to Lord विष्णु), द्वारका has been highly eulogised in the Hindu religious works, especially the पुराणस्.
The main temple is that of Dvārakādhīśa or Raṇchoḍjī (Śrī कृष्ण). The original temple could have been built during the Gupta period (A. D. 320-525) and repaired during the age of the Solaṅkis (9th to 13th cent. A. D.). It is situated on the bank of the गोमती which is not a river but the back-waters of the Arabian sea. The main dome or tower is 42 metres (140 ft.) in height. The large मण्डप (open hall) has sixty pillars. There is enough space for प्रदक्षिण or circumambulation. In the garbhamandir or sanctum there is the beautiful image of कृष्ण made of black stone, 90 cms (3 ft.) in height, with four arms. Pilgrims are permitted to touch the feet of the image and offer tulasi (holy basil) leaves.
Deity at the TempleOther images in the temple campus are those of अम्बा, बलराम, त्रिविक्रम and प्रद्युम्न.
There is a separate temple for शिव as ‘Kuśeśvara महादेव’.
There are nine bathing ghāṭs for pilgrims such as Saṅgama-ghāṭ, नारायण ghāṭ, वासुदेव-ghāṭ, Goghāṭ and so on.
There is a small lake of salt water near one of the ghāṭs, called ‘Niṣpāpa-sarovara’. A bath here has been considered almost compulsory.
Other temples in द्वारका are those of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and वासुदेव. The temple of Nāgeśvara-लिङ्ग (Śiva) is an ancient one.
Pilgrims sometimes undertake what is known as ‘Dvārakāpradakṣiṇa,’ circumambulation of the whole place for which a particular order is prescribed.
Śrī कृष्ण-जन्माष्टमी is the biggest festival observed in the main temple.
There is an ancient monastery—the Śāradāpīṭha—established by Śaṅkarā-cārya (A. D. 788-820) here.

dvāra
(‘that [through which] one goes out of the [house]’)
------------------------------------------
The science of building construction, architecture and town-planning was well-developed in ancient and medieval India. Works like the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (300 B. C.), the Mānasāra (revised edition, 11th cent. A. D.), Mayamata, Mānasollāsa of king Someśvara (A. D. 1126-1138) and various पुराणस् like the Agnipurāṇa and the Matsyapurāṇa contain a lot of information on this subject.
Location and construction of the dvāras (entrances and doors) of buildings was considered as very important, not only from the standpoint of safety and beauty, but also of auspiciousness.
A village or a town must have dvāras in the four cardinal directions and also four, in between, in the corners.
Buildings too should have four main dvāras or doors on the four sides. Smaller doors can be constructed as per convenience.
The main entrance door in a building should not be kept in the middle, but on either side only. But, in the case of temples it should be in the middle only.
The most general rule for the dimension is that the height of the door should be twice the width (h = 2w).
The doors are generally decorated with the carvings of leaves and creepers. The relief figures of गणेश, सरस्वती and other deities should be there on both sides of a door.
Though it is advisable to have two shutters, the door may have a single shutter also.
The above-mentioned works give detailed measurements and instructions for the construction of doors.
